label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
in_my_words: Each agent wakes on its own clock, may only touch the files on its page of rules, has its plan and its result read by a second agent, and anyone can drop a hold file to stop everything, so the person could walk away for nine hours.
why: I came asking whether my own team could run like this, and chapter 3 shows the checking and arguing that makes leaving it alone believable. The do-this-now steps are small enough to try. I want to know what actually broke, and what the empty chair was.

by_section.why: Short and concrete. The setup is easy to picture: an empty repository, a brief and one page of rules.
by_section.quote: a brief and one page of rules

by_section.why: Four agents, three glossary terms and a figure arrive at once. I stopped to hold dev, conductor, deck and ruv-sgit apart. The one-line owner statements help, but the word 'check' is also called 'the gate' and I nearly missed that it was one thing.
by_section.quote: A check is a test every change must pass before it goes out (the team called it the gate).

by_section.why: A Wardley map described in words with no picture on my phone. I got the point from the single line below it, not from the map.
by_section.quote: the bottom of the chain was already ordinary, so the top could be built in a day

by_section.section: The clock and the five steps
by_section.why: This is what I came for: a clock, a hold anyone can pull, and the five steps in plain words. I could copy it for my own team.
by_section.quote: It looks slow written down. The checking is what let nobody watch.

by_section.why: The honest limit lands well, and a first wake that closes partial is believable. The 'reviewer is the same kind of agent' preface is the useful caution.
by_section.quote: a second reading, not a second identity

by_section.why: Quick and clear. The researcher and designer are introduced only by a clause each, and the designer barely sticks.
Practical and doable in a gap between meetings.
by_section.quote: You do not need six agents. You need the page the first one read.

by_section.why: States the claim and what holds it up before the evidence. Without the chart on a phone the nine-hours claim rests on trust, but it is clear.
by_section.quote: For nine hours I started nothing.

by_section.why: Strongest scene for my question: an agent disputes its own checker from the rules and the checker retracts. It shows the checks are not rubber stamps.
by_section.quote: I am not asking for an exception; I am asking you to read the line again.

by_section.why: Four incidents with four different pairings (deck to ruv-sgit, deck's reviewer to deck, designer to itself, conductor to ruv-sgit) in one section. The names blur and the second incident is hard to follow. The at-sign story needs the reader to know the team counts work by name.
Clear loop of ask, look, change, look again; the times make it concrete. 'All nine were on stage' lands, though I could not name the nine.
by_section.quote: I looked, I asked, they changed it, I looked again.

by_section.why: Good, and the storyteller finally gets a voice. The dispute on the record beside the editor's decision is the part I would copy.
by_section.quote: a story that hides the strongest argument against it is not one I want to tell

by_section.why: A neat safeguard: a passed-on approval is not accepted. Short and memorable. Studio is only a name here, with no earlier introduction.
by_section.quote: My session would not take a relayed word for his, so I asked him myself.
Give one small thing to somebody else today

best_line: It looks slow written down. The checking is what let nobody watch.
worst_moment: Sent back, and owned: four incidents in one section, so I lost who sent what to whom.
cut: Trim 'Sent back, and owned' to two incidents, probably the picture sent back and the designer owning its table. Drop the at-sign episode or give it one line on why the name counts work. Consider cutting the Wardley map prose to two sentences.
notes: Unexplained terms I met: 'hold' is explained, but 'wake' and 'debrief' are glossed in a box I might skip on a phone. The empty chair promise ('it comes back at the end') makes me want chapter 4. Dramatised lines mixed with real record lines worked because of the (record) marker. I never learned who the storyteller, motion and studio are for, and the cast bar is described but I cannot see it. For my team, the missing piece is what the agents cost to run and who paid for it.
